title: Fabrication And Characterization Of High-Quality Nb/Al-AlO$_x$/Nb Cross-Type Josephson Tunnel Junctions Utilising CMP-based Planarisation Techniques
authors: Alexander Stoll, Andreas Reifenberger, Daniel Hengstler, Andreas Fleischmann, Christian Enss
abstract: Josephson tunnel junctions (JJs) are the fundamental building blocks of today's most advanced superconducting electronic components, such as qubits and superconducting quantum interference devices (SQUIDs). Given the ongoing demand for scalability of these devices on the wafer-scale, it is crucial to control the fabrication process as precisely as possible to ensure uniform quality and reproducibility. Today, window-type JJs are often used in the production of DC SQUIDs and while they are reliable and reproducible, they suffer from alignment inaccuracies caused by photolithography and unavoidable parasitic capacitances, thus limiting the energy sensitivity of DC SQUIDs. These problems can be circumvented by producing JJs with cross-type geometry, which allows for smaller junction areas and eliminates parasitic capacitances. Here we discuss the fabrication of Nb/Al-AlOx/Nb-based cross-type JJs, where the trilayer is embedded in sputter-deposited SiO$_2$ to allow for planarisation of the structures and to ensure the reliable insulation of the sidewalls of the bottom electrode. Instead of lift-off processes that require a lot of time and potentially leave unwanted wings along the edges of microstructures behind that might compromise subsequent layers, we use chemical-mechanical polishing (CMP) for the removal of excess SiO$_2$. This is not only much faster, but produces smooth and uniform surfaces, which in turn effectively improves the reliability of our JJ production process resulting in a high yield of over $90\,\%$ on wafer-scale. In addition, we discuss the influence of fabrication details on the quality and electrical properties of our JJs with different junction areas down to $1\,\mathrm{μm} \times 1\,\mathrm{μm}$ distributed across the wafer and extract the junction specific quality parameters from their IV-characteristics and their Fraunhofer patterns.
summary: This paper details a fabrication breakthrough for superconducting Josephson junctions using a cross-type geometry. By replacing traditional lift-off processes with Chemical-Mechanical Polishing (CMP) for planarization, the authors achieved high yield and excellent uniformity on a wafer scale. This advancement is critical for the reliable scaling of superconducting quantum devices.
main_problem: The paper addresses the need for scalable, high-quality Josephson tunnel junctions (JJs) for superconducting electronics, overcoming limitations associated with traditional window-type JJs.
main_result: A novel fabrication scheme using Chemical-Mechanical Polishing (CMP) successfully produces high-yield, cross-type Nb/Al-AlOx/Nb JJs down to $1 \mu	ext{m} 	imes 1 \mu	ext{m}$ on a wafer scale.
method: The core method involves depositing the superconducting trilayer, embedding it in $	ext{SiO}_2$, and then using CMP to planarize the excess oxide, replacing slower and less reliable lift-off processes.
model_or_system: The physical system is a cross-type Josephson tunnel junction ($	ext{Nb/Al-AlO}_x/	ext{Nb}$), which is a fundamental building block for superconducting quantum devices like qubits and SQUIDs.
key_observables: IV-characteristics, Fraunhofer patterns, critical current ($I_c$), normal state resistance ($R_N$), and junction area ($A_{JJ}$).
important_parameters: Junction areas down to $1 \mu	ext{m} 	imes 1 \mu	ext{m}$; high yield ($>90\%$); specific CMP parameters (e.g., slurry type, pressures).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the smooth profile edges created by CMP are appropriate for modeling the current distribution in the junction.
figures_summary: Figures show schematic fabrication steps highlighting CMP use, SEM images of planarized junctions, light microscope views of cross-type JJs, and electrical measurement setups (e.g., four-wire measurement).
paper_structure: The paper details the fabrication process, emphasizing the CMP planarization step over lift-off. It then presents electrical characterization using IV curves and magnetic field measurements (Fraunhofer patterns) to confirm high quality and scalability.
why_interesting: The work directly relates to the physical realization of superconducting quantum circuits, providing crucial engineering data on device fabrication necessary for scaling quantum processors.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Schematic of our fabrication process of cross-type JJs utilising the CMP process. a) Nb/Al-AlOx/Nb-trilayer is deposited on the substrate. b) The trilayer is microstructured into a stripe using photolithography and etching. c) SiO2 is deposited to insulate the bottom electrode from the subsequent wiring layer. d) The trilayer is planarised by CMP. e) The Nb wiring layer is deposited perpendicular to the trilayer structure and cross-type JJ area defined via etching of the wiring layer and the top electrode of the trilayer. f) Wet-etching of the Al-AlOx layer and removal of the photoresist.

Figure 3: SEM image of a 2 µm wide and 200 nm high etched Nb structure with the positive-tone photoresist AZ MIR 701 on top, depicting the achieved vertical sidewalls of the etched Nb film. The light and dark stripes seen in the photoresist sidewall result from in- terference between the incident and reflected light during laser lithography.

Figure 2: Mechanical stress map of a 200 nm thick Nb film deposited onto a 3 inch Si wafer. This was obtained by measuring the height profiles along 60 mm-long lines at nine different wafer orienta- tions (in steps of 20°, measured with a Bruker Dektak XT profilometer2). Measurements were performed before and after Nb deposition to cal- culate the film stress. The colour coding of the map shows the interpolation of those nine lines.
Figure 4: Scanning electron microscope (SEM) picture of a planarised 2 µm wide Nb/Al-AlOx/Nb trilayer, which corresponds to step d) in figure 1).
Figure 5: Light microscope picture of a 2 × 2 µm2 cross-type JJ fabricated with the scheme shown in figure 1.
